title: YouTube
brief: Design a video platform like YouTube, where anyone can upload and anyone can watch. Unlike a curated catalog, new video arrives constantly, most of it is rarely watched, and a few videos get enormous traffic. This page is a general design for a system like it, not a description of how any real company builds it.

functional: Upload a large video, and resume if the connection drops.
Watch any public video at a quality that fits the connection.
Search videos by title and description.
See a view count, and comment on a video.
Get suggested videos to watch next.
Block content that is abusive or copyrighted.

nonFunctional.name: Upload to playable
nonFunctional.target: A typical video is watchable within minutes of upload

nonFunctional.name: Playback start
nonFunctional.target: Starts in under 2 seconds at the 95th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: An accepted upload is never lost

nonFunctional.name: View counts
nonFunctional.target: Approximate and a few minutes behind is fine

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: Watching stays up even if upload or search is down

estimate.note: Assumptions you can move. Two numbers shape the design: new video to process and store each day, and view events per second. One database write per view would crush it, so views are batched.

inputs.label: Hours of video uploaded per minute
Views folded into one count write
inputs.note: Average over the flush window. Popular videos fold many, rare ones fold few.

outputs.label: Transcode tasks per second
outputs.note: 10 second chunks, each encoded once per rendition.

outputs.label: View writes, one per view
outputs.note: Hot videos would all hit one row.

outputs.label: Views that reach the origin
outputs.note: The long tail. Each one is a cold read.

api.does: Opens an upload session and returns a session URL. Bytes go to the upload service, not the app servers.
Sends one chunk. After a drop, a status query tells the client where to resume.
Returns title, counts, comments preview and the manifest URL.
Returns ranked video cards that match the query.
Records a view event. Fire and forget, and it never blocks playback.
Adds a comment. Listing is paged, newest or top first.

data.fields: videoId, ownerId, title, status, manifestUrl, createdAt
data.store: Sharded key-value or SQL store by videoId.
data.why: Every read is by id. Status moves from uploaded to processing to live or blocked.
Large immutable files. Cheap per byte and cache friendly.

data.store: In-memory buffer, flushed to the video store.
data.why: Incremented a huge number of times. Batch in memory and flush as one add.
Always read as a page of one video's comments. Hot videos need a cached first page.

evolution.title: Upload a file, serve it back
evolution.problem: Start with what works: the app server accepts a video file, stores it, and sends the same file to every viewer.
evolution.change: One server, one stored file per video. Anyone can upload and anyone can watch, but only one quality.

evolution.title: Resumable upload
evolution.problem: Videos are gigabytes and mobile connections drop. Pushing the whole file through the app servers ties them up, and one failure restarts a long upload.
evolution.change: A dedicated upload service opens a session and takes the file in chunks. The client asks where it stopped and resumes from there. Chunks land in object storage, so app servers never carry the bytes.

evolution.title: A transcoding DAG
evolution.problem: The upload is in whatever format the creator had. It is too big for phones and cannot adapt to bandwidth. One machine encoding a long video takes ages.
evolution.change: A finished upload queues a job: split into chunks, encode each chunk into every rendition in parallel, stitch the results, make thumbnails, write a manifest. This is a DAG, a graph of tasks where each waits only for its inputs.
evolution.numbers: tasks per second and storage per day in the estimator

evolution.title: Metadata, search and comments
evolution.problem: Listing videos by scanning storage is impossible, and people need to find videos and discuss them.
evolution.change: Keep video records in a metadata store keyed by id. Feed a search index from it. Store comments by video in their own store so a busy comment section does not slow the watch page.

evolution.title: CDN for the head, origin for the tail
evolution.problem: Watching is the bulk of the bytes. A small share of videos draws most of the views, and the rest are watched rarely.
evolution.change: Serve segments through CDN edges that keep popular videos. A rare video misses and is read from storage. Do not push the long tail to the edge. It would fill caches with things nobody asks for.
evolution.numbers: the share served from edge decides origin load

evolution.title: Batched view counts and suggestions
evolution.problem: At 100K views per second, one database write per view is 100K writes per second, and a viral video makes them all hit one row.
evolution.change: App servers send a view ping to a counter that adds up in memory and flushes a total every few seconds. The same stream of signals feeds the recommender, which writes candidate lists back. Counts are approximate and slightly late, and that is fine.
evolution.numbers: view writes before and after batching

evolution.title: Abuse and copyright as an async stage
evolution.problem: Some uploads are harmful or copied. Scanning inline would make every upload wait, and checks improve over time.
evolution.change: After transcoding, a separate worker fingerprints the video, runs checks and then publishes or blocks it in the metadata store. Uploads are accepted at once, and a video becomes public only when the checks pass.

steps.say: The client opens an upload session and sends the file in chunks to the upload service.
Each chunk is written to object storage. If the link drops, the client asks what was received and continues from there.
When the last chunk lands, the upload service queues a transcode job.
Workers split the video, encode chunks into every rendition in parallel and stitch them.
Renditions, thumbnails and the manifest are written to object storage.
The abuse stage fingerprints the video and runs its checks.
If clean, the video is marked live in the metadata store. The search index is updated from it.
The client asks the app servers for the watch page of a video.
The server reads the video record, with title, counts and manifest URL.
It reads the first page of comments from their own store.
The player fetches the manifest and segments from the CDN edge.
A popular video is already cached. A rare one misses and the edge reads it from storage.
The page sends a view ping. The counter adds it in memory and does not write to the database yet.
Every few seconds the counter flushes one total per video to the metadata store.

deepDives.title: Counting views
deepDives.question: How do we count views without a write per view?

options.name: Write on every view
options.cons: 100K writes per second, and a viral video makes one hot row everyone fights over.

options.name: Batch in memory, flush
options.pros: Writes drop by the batch size. Hot rows get one add per flush.
options.cons: A crash loses the last few seconds. Counts lag.

options.name: Event log, aggregate later
options.pros: Every event is kept. Allows spam filtering and exact recounts.
options.cons: More moving parts and a larger delay before the number moves.

deepDives.pick: Batch for the live number, log for the truth
deepDives.because: Nobody needs the exact number every second. Show the batched count, and log events so a slower job can remove bots and fix totals.

deepDives.title: What the CDN keeps
deepDives.question: Which videos belong at the edge?

options.name: Everything everywhere
options.cons: Storage cost is huge and most copies are never used.

options.name: Pull on demand with LRU
options.pros: Automatic. Edges hold what was recently watched.
options.cons: One-off views of rare videos push out hot ones.

options.name: Admit on repeat, keep the head
options.pros: Cache a segment only after a few requests. The tail stays out.
options.cons: The second viewer of a rising video still misses.

deepDives.because: Popularity is extremely skewed. Admitting only repeated requests protects the cache from the tail, and a mid-tier cache softens the misses.

deepDives.title: Transcoding as a DAG
deepDives.question: How do we make encoding fast and safe?

options.name: One job per video
options.cons: A long video takes hours, and a failure restarts everything.

options.name: Chunk-level DAG
options.pros: Chunks encode in parallel. A failed chunk is retried alone. Time depends on chunk count, not video length.
options.cons: Needs a scheduler, stitching and care at chunk boundaries.

deepDives.because: Output names come from the video id and chunk number, so a retry overwrites with the same bytes. Start a video's lower renditions first so it can be watched early.

deepDives.title: Abuse and copyright checks
deepDives.question: When do we check an upload, and what do we do on a match?

options.name: Block until clean
options.cons: Every upload waits on the slowest check.

options.name: Publish, then scan
options.cons: Bad content is visible until found.

options.name: Scan async, publish when clear
options.pros: Uploads accepted at once. Public only after checks pass.
options.cons: A delay before going live. Needs a review queue for edge cases.

deepDives.because: Fingerprint matching and classifiers can run alongside transcoding. New checks can be re-run over stored videos without touching the upload path.

failures.impact: One chunk of one rendition is missing, and the video cannot go live.
failures.fix: Tasks are idempotent and time-limited. The scheduler retries on another worker. Mark the video live only when every required rendition is complete.

failures.impact: A creator would have to start a multi-gigabyte upload again.
failures.fix: Chunks are durable the moment they are acknowledged. Session state lives in a store, so any upload server can answer where the client resumed.

failures.what: Viral video floods one origin object
failures.impact: Thousands of edges miss at once and hammer one storage key.
failures.fix: Collapse concurrent misses into one fetch, put a mid-tier cache between edges and storage, and replicate the hot objects.

failures.impact: Counts from the last few seconds are lost.
failures.fix: Accept it for the live number. Events are also logged, so a periodic job recomputes totals and fixes drift.

failures.impact: A new video does not show in search for a while.
failures.fix: Index from change events, and show the owner a direct link. A short delay is acceptable for discovery.

scaling.limit: Storage grows by petabytes a day
scaling.lever: Keep fewer renditions for rarely watched videos, move cold videos to cheaper storage and re-encode older uploads with better codecs.
Scale workers with queue depth, use spot capacity and prioritise new uploads from creators with fresh audiences.
More edge sites and ISP caches for the head, and tune admission so the cache holds only what repeats.

recap.key: Process each upload once through a parallel transcoding DAG, serve the popular head from the edge and the long tail from storage, and batch view counts instead of writing one per view.
recap.numbers: 500 hours per minute is 720K hours a day, about 3.9 PB of renditions a day. 100K views per second is 1K writes per second after batching 100 per write.
moves: Resumable chunked upload straight to object storage
CDN for the head, origin for the tail
Batch view counts and run abuse checks asynchronously
